mainTopic: The end of the כוי proof, and the source and nature of the עינוי (fasting) of יום כיפור, with related אגדה about the מן
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier argument. The גמרא had tried to support ריש לקיש about חצי שיעור from the fact that a פסוק includes the כוי. The גמרא rejects that proof: a כוי is its own creature (בריה בפני עצמה), so a פסוק can include it even though a mere doubt would not need one. Then a new topic begins: what does 'תענו את נפשותיכם' on יום כיפור mean? Two ברייתות compare עינוי to מלאכה. The first says affliction is passive and the same for everyone. The second links it to eating, and then climbs a ladder from פיגול and נותר up to קדשים, showing that every kind of food is forbidden. Further proofs come from 'I will destroy that soul' and from the school of רבי ישמעאל, who learns from the hunger in the desert. After rejecting comparisons to לבן's daughters and to Egypt, the גמרא concludes that a Heaven-sent affliction is learned from a Heaven-sent affliction. The amud ends with אגדה about why the מן was an affliction and about the value of seeing your food. It then begins a new dispute between רבי אמי and רבי אסי about wine, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The proof is rejected because a כוי is its own creature
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the attempted support for ריש לקיש. It says a כוי may be a unique creature, not just a doubtful case.
steps.simpleTranslation: A כוי is a creature of its own kind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is knocking down the earlier proof for ריש לקיש. It says the כוי needed its own פסוק because it is a unique creature, not because it is a doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier argument went like this: a כוי is only a ספק (doubt), and a פסוק is never needed to include a doubt. So the inclusion must be only מדרבנן, and the same would be true of חצי שיעור. The rejection answers that a כוי may be its own category entirely. That is a real, definite thing, and a definite thing can need a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal whose status is unclear: wild animal (חיה) or domestic animal (בהמה)
A creature of its own kind, a separate category
Less than the full measure of a forbidden food

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא is ruling here on whether חצי שיעור is permitted. It is only saying this specific proof for ריש לקיש does not work.

phrases.english: A koy is a creature of its own kind.
phrases.notes: Continues the rejection begun on the previous amud ('perhaps a כוי is different')

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support for ריש לקיש brought on the previous amud
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from כוי. It does not reject ריש לקיש's position itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the כוי is a mere doubt. It may actually be a separate category, which would justify a פסוק.

steps.title: Proof from רב אידי בר אבין that a כוי is a separate creature
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves that a כוי must be treated as its own creature. Otherwise רב אידי בר אבין's teaching from 'כל' would make no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you do not say so, what about what רב אידי בר אבין said: 'כל' also comes to include the כוי? If a כוי is just a doubt, would a פסוק be needed to include a doubt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its rejection with a source. רב אידי בר אבין used the word 'כל' (about blood) to include a כוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסוק is never needed just to include a doubtful case. רב אידי בר אבין did use a פסוק for the כוי, so he must have seen it as a definite separate creature. That supports the claim made in step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you do not say so
An אמורא who derived the inclusion of כוי from the word 'כל'

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין:
phrases.english: then that which Rav Idi bar Avin said:
also 'all' comes to include the koy,
if the koy is merely a doubt,
would a verse be needed to include a doubt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection in step 1
steps.raayaObject: That a כוי is a separate creature (בריה בפני עצמה)
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב אידי בר אבין's derivation of כוי from 'כל' in the פסוק about blood

steps.title: A unique creature is different, so the proof for ריש לקיש falls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the כוי is different because it is a unique creature. So the earlier ברייתא proves nothing about חצי שיעור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a unique creature is different. Here too, a unique creature is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the argument. Just as רב אידי's teaching about blood treats the כוי as a unique creature, the same explanation works for חלב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the כוי is a real category, a פסוק could include it on a Torah level. That tells us nothing about a doubt or about חצי שיעור. The attempted support for ריש לקיש is cancelled.
steps.whatToRemember: The כוי is treated as a בריה בפני עצמה. So including it by a פסוק cannot prove that חצי שיעור is only rabbinically forbidden.

phrases.english: Rather, a unique creature is different,
here too, a unique creature is different.
phrases.notes: Here = the ברייתא about חלב of a כוי

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof in step 2
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא about כוי cannot be used to support ריש לקיש about חצי שיעור.

steps.title: Affliction on יום הכיפורים is passive, like the ban on מלאכה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that 'תענו את נפשותיכם' does not mean actively making yourself suffer. It means holding back from actions, just like מלאכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: 'You shall afflict your souls.' I might think a person should sit in the sun or in the cold to suffer. So the פסוק says: 'And you shall not do any labor.' Just as labor is 'sit and do nothing,' so too affliction is 'sit and do nothing.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. A ברייתא explains what kind of affliction the Torah wants on יום הכיפורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the comparison, you might think you must actively cause yourself pain. The פסוק places עינוי next to מלאכה, and מלאכה is kept by refraining. So עינוי is also kept by refraining, for example from eating and drinking.

keyTerms.meaning: Sit and do nothing: a passive commandment

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic nature of the יום הכיפורים affliction. It is refraining, not self-inflicted pain.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
'You shall afflict your souls,'
I might think one should sit in the sun or in the cold
in order to suffer —
the verse states: 'And you shall not do any labor.'
Just as labor is 'sit and do nothing,'

phrases.aramaic: אַף עִנּוּי נֶפֶשׁ שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה.
phrases.english: so too affliction of the soul is 'sit and do nothing.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the כוי discussion ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The affliction of יום הכיפורים is fulfilled passively, by refraining, like the ban on מלאכה.

steps.title: Maybe 'passive' means leaving someone in discomfort
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. Maybe 'sit and do nothing' means that someone already uncomfortable in the sun or shade should simply stay there.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: if someone is sitting in the sun and is hot, we do not tell him, 'Get up and sit in the shade.' If he is sitting in the shade and is cold, we do not tell him, 'Get up and sit in the sun.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions what the ברייתא proved. Even passive affliction could mean being told to stay in an uncomfortable spot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Staying put in the heat or cold is also 'sit and do nothing.' So the comparison to מלאכה may not rule out discomfort from sun or cold. Maybe it only rules out actively going there.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵימָא: הֵיכָא דְּיָתֵיב בְּשִׁימְשָׁא וְחָיֵים לֵיהּ
phrases.english: But say: where he sits in the sun and it is hot for him,

phrases.aramaic: לָא נֵימָא לֵיהּ קוּם תּוּב בְּטוּלָּא,
phrases.english: we do not tell him, 'Get up, sit in the shade,'
if he sits in the shade and it is cold for him,

phrases.aramaic: לָא נֵימָא לֵיהּ קוּם תּוּב בְּשִׁימְשָׁא!
phrases.english: we do not tell him, 'Get up, sit in the sun!'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: הֵיכָא דְּיָתֵיב בְּשִׁימְשָׁא וְחָיֵים לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of the ברייתא in step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that the comparison to מלאכה rules out sun and cold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Staying in discomfort is also passive. So 'שב ואל תעשה' does not by itself rule out discomfort.

steps.title: Like מלאכה, affliction does not depend on personal situations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that עינוי must be like מלאכה in every way. The law of מלאכה does not change by circumstance, so עינוי does not either.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is similar to labor: just as with labor you made no distinctions, so too with affliction you make no distinctions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in step 5. It extends the comparison to מלאכה one step further.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on מלאכה is the same for everyone, no matter where they happen to be sitting. So עינוי must also be a fixed obligation that is the same for everyone. It cannot be tied to whether a person happens to be hot or cold.

phrases.english: Similar to labor:
just as with labor you did not distinguish,
so too with affliction you shall not distinguish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Passive discomfort, like staying in the sun, could count as עינוי
steps.terutzMaskana: עינוי is uniform like מלאכה and does not depend on personal circumstances, so sun and cold play no role.

steps.title: A second ברייתא: affliction parallels a ban that carries כרת
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא uses the same פסוק differently. Just as מלאכה carries כרת elsewhere, עינוי refers to something that carries כרת elsewhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא taught: 'You shall afflict your souls.' I might think one should sit in the sun and the cold and suffer. So the פסוק says: 'And you shall not do any labor.' Just as labor is something that carries a punishment elsewhere, so too affliction refers to something that carries a punishment elsewhere.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא with a different angle on the same comparison. It sets up a question about which forbidden thing is meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the comparison is not about being passive. It is about punishment: מלאכה carries כרת on שבת. So עינוי must relate to an act that elsewhere carries כרת, which points to eating.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in another ברייתא
One is liable for it (here, to כרת)

phrases.english: It was taught in another baraita: 'You shall afflict your souls,'
I might think one should sit in the sun and the cold and suffer —
the verse states: 'And you shall not do any labor.'

phrases.aramaic: מָה מְלָאכָה דָּבָר שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עָלָיו בִּמְקוֹם אַחֵר,
phrases.english: Just as labor is something for which one is liable elsewhere,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עִנּוּי נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עָלָיו בִּמְקוֹם אַחֵר,
phrases.english: so too affliction refers to something for which one is liable elsewhere.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different reading of the same comparison
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עינוי refers to holding back from an act that carries כרת in another context.

steps.title: Which act is meant?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks which act, liable to כרת elsewhere, it is talking about.
steps.simpleTranslation: And which is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks what it means by 'something that carries כרת elsewhere.' It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison so far only gives a general rule. Now the ברייתא needs to name the specific act it has in mind.

phrases.english: And which is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the specific case behind the general rule in step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which forbidden act, liable to כרת elsewhere, does the comparison point to?

steps.title: The answer: eating פיגול and נותר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that it means פיגול and נותר. Eating them carries כרת, so עינוי is about eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is פיגול and נותר.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא names the case. Eating פיגול and נותר carries כרת, which shows that the affliction of יום הכיפורים is about not eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating פיגול or נותר is punished with כרת. Linking עינוי to them teaches that affliction means refraining from eating, which also carries כרת on יום הכיפורים. Sitting in the sun or cold is not included.

keyTerms.meaning: A קרבן made invalid by an improper intent about when it would be eaten; eating it carries כרת
Meat of a קרבן left past its allowed time; eating it carries כרת

steps.whatToRemember: Both ברייתות agree that sitting in the sun or cold is not the required עינוי. The first says affliction is passive and uniform, like מלאכה. The second says it parallels eating that carries כרת, such as פיגול and נותר.

phrases.english: This is piggul and notar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: פיגול and נותר, whose eating carries כרת. This links עינוי to refraining from eating.

steps.title: Expanding from פיגול and נותר to טבל
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא might have included only פיגול and נותר, which carry כרת, and left out טבל, which does not. The verse expands the rule to include טבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might think I should include only פיגול and נותר, since they carry כרת, and not include טבל, which does not carry כרת. So the verse says 'תענו' and 'ועניתם את נפשותיכם'. This extra language includes more.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא begins a ladder. It proposes a limit, that only כרת foods are included, and then uses the extra verse language to push past that limit to include טבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 linked עינוי to foods with a כרת penalty, so a learner might think only those foods are banned. טבל is a lighter prohibition with no כרת, so it seems it should be left out. The verse's repeated wording of affliction tells us to include it anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I will bring in', meaning I will include this in the rule
Produce from which the required tithes and gifts have not yet been taken
'The verse teaches', which introduces the Torah's answer
'It included', meaning the verse widens the rule to cover more cases

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does NOT say טבל is permitted on other days. Everyone agrees טבל is forbidden all year. The only question is whether the special עינוי ban of יום כיפור applies to it. The 'I will not include' line is only a proposed limit, and the verse rejects it.

phrases.english: I will include piggul and notar, which carry karet,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַטֶּבֶל שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּכָרֵת,
phrases.english: but I will not include untithed produce, which does not carry karet;
phrases.notes: This is a proposed limit, and the verse is about to reject it.

phrases.english: therefore the verse states: 'You shall afflict' (Leviticus 16:29),
and 'You shall afflict your souls' (Leviticus 16:31): it included more.
phrases.notes: The repeated affliction language serves as an expansion.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבִיא פִּגּוּל וְנוֹתָר שֶׁהֵן בְּכָרֵת, וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַטֶּבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the כרת foods from Step 9 and widens the rule past them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The עינוי ban on יום כיפור includes טבל, even though it carries no כרת.

steps.title: Expanding from טבל to נבילה
steps.stepSummary: Maybe only טבל is included, since it carries מיתה בידי שמים, and not נבילה, which does not. The verse expands the rule to include נבילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might think I should include טבל, which carries a death penalty from Heaven, and not include נבילה, which does not carry that penalty. So the verse says 'תענו' and 'ועניתם את נפשותיכם'. This extra language includes more.
steps.whatsHappening: The ladder goes down one more rung. A new limit is proposed, that only foods with a heavenly death penalty are included, and the verse pushes past it to include נבילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each rung finds some feature that the last included food has and the next food lacks. Here the feature is מיתה בידי שמים, which טבל has and נבילה lacks. The verse's extra wording still includes נבילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Death at the hands of Heaven, a penalty given by God and not by a court
An animal that died without proper kosher slaughter

phrases.english: I will include untithed produce, which carries death at the hand of Heaven,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַנְּבֵילָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ בְּמִיתָה —
phrases.english: but I will not include an unslaughtered carcass, which does not carry death;
therefore the verse states: 'You shall afflict',
and 'You shall afflict your souls': it included more.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבִיא הַטֶּבֶל שֶׁהוּא בְּמִיתָה וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַנְּבֵילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 10. טבל is now included, so the next lighter food is tested.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The עינוי ban includes נבילה, even though it carries no death penalty.

steps.title: Expanding from נבילה to ordinary food (חולין)
steps.stepSummary: Maybe only foods with a לאו, such as נבילה, are included, and not ordinary חולין. The verse expands the rule to include even permitted, everyday food.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might think I should include נבילה, which is forbidden by a negative commandment, and not include ordinary food, which is not forbidden at all. So the verse says 'תענו' and 'ועניתם את נפשותיכם'. This extra language includes more.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the ladder reaches regular, permitted food. The proposed limit is that only foods with some prohibition are included, and the verse includes normal food too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, every included food was already forbidden all year. חולין has no prohibition at all, so it seems furthest from the rule. The verse still includes it, which is the main practical point: on יום כיפור, even regular food is banned.

keyTerms.meaning: A negative commandment in the Torah ('do not')
Ordinary, non-sacred food that is normally permitted

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the step that makes all regular food forbidden on יום כיפור. Everything after this deals with special holy foods.

phrases.english: I will include a carcass, which is under a negative commandment,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַחוּלִּין שֶׁאֵינָן בְּלָאו?
phrases.english: but will I not include non-sacred food, which is not under a negative commandment?
therefore the verse states: 'You shall afflict',
and 'You shall afflict your souls': it included more.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבִיא אֶת הַנְּבֵילָה שֶׁהוּא בְּלָאו, וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַחוּלִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 11. נבילה is now included, so the next food tested is permitted food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The עינוי ban includes ordinary permitted food (חולין).

steps.title: Expanding from חולין to תרומה
steps.stepSummary: Maybe חולין is included, since there is no מצוה to eat it, but תרומה is not, since a כהן has a מצוה to eat it. The verse includes תרומה too.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might think I should include ordinary food, which you have no מצוה to eat, and not include תרומה, which a כהן has a מצוה to eat. So the verse says 'תענו' and 'ועניתם את נפשותיכם'. This extra language includes more.
steps.whatsHappening: The direction of the ladder changes. Now the question is about food that comes with a מצוה to eat it, and the verse says even that is banned on יום כיפור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to here the test was how forbidden a food is. Now the test is the opposite: a food you are commanded to eat might seem to override the fast. The verse includes תרומה anyway, so the fast wins.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Arise and eat', meaning a positive מצוה to eat this food
The holy portion of produce given to a כהן, which he is commanded to eat

phrases.english: I will include non-sacred food, which carries no command to 'arise and eat',

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַתְּרוּמָה שֶׁהִיא בְּקוּם אֱכוֹל,
phrases.english: but I will not include teruma, which carries a command to 'arise and eat';
therefore the verse states: 'You shall afflict',
and 'You shall afflict your souls': it included more.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבִיא הַחוּלִּין שֶׁאֵינָן בְּקוּם אֱכוֹל, וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַתְּרוּמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 12. חולין is now included, so the next food tested has a מצוה to eat it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The עינוי ban includes תרומה, even though a כהן has a מצוה to eat it.

steps.title: Final expansion to sacred offerings: all food is included
steps.stepSummary: Maybe תרומה is included, since it has no time limit, but קדשים are not, since they fall under בל תותירו and must be eaten in time. The verse includes even קדשים, so every food is banned on יום כיפור.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might think I should include תרומה, which has no rule of 'do not leave over', and not include holy offerings, which do have the rule of 'do not leave over'. So the verse says 'תענו' and 'ועניתם את נפשותיכם'. This extra language includes more.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last and strongest rung of the ladder. Even holy sacrificial meat, which must be eaten before its deadline, is included, so the ban now covers every kind of food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קדשים have an even stronger push to be eaten than תרומה, because leaving them over breaks the law of בל תותירו. Even so, the verse includes them in the יום כיפור ban. That completes the proof that no food is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Do not leave over', the ban on leaving sacrificial meat uneaten past its time
Holy sacrificial meat that must be eaten within a set time

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא uses the repeated affliction verses as a ladder. It goes from כרת foods, to טבל, to נבילה, to ordinary חולין, to תרומה, and finally to קדשים. The result: eating any food at all on יום כיפור violates עינוי.

phrases.aramaic: אָבִיא אֶת הַתְּרוּמָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ בְּבַל תּוֹתִירוּ,
phrases.english: I will include teruma, which is not subject to 'you shall not leave over',

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַקֳּדָשִׁים שֶׁהֵן בְּבַל תּוֹתִירוּ,
phrases.english: but I will not include sacred food, which is subject to 'you shall not leave over';
therefore the verse states: 'You shall afflict',
and 'You shall afflict your souls': it included more.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבִיא אֶת הַתְּרוּמָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ בְּבַל תּוֹתִירוּ, וְלֹא אָבִיא אֶת הַקֳּדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The final rung, built on Step 13. It closes the whole ladder that started from פיגול and נותר.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Every type of food, from forbidden food to holy sacrificial meat, is included in the ban on eating on יום כיפור.

steps.title: Extra proof: the affliction that can destroy a soul
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a further proof. The verse 'I will destroy that soul' shows that the עינוי of יום כיפור is one that can kill a person, which means not eating and drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want to say something against this, look at what the verse says: 'I will destroy that soul.' So the affliction is one that destroys a soul. Which affliction is that? Not eating and drinking.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a second, stronger proof that the עינוי of יום כיפור means not eating and drinking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah describes the punishment with the words 'I will destroy that soul.' This hints that the affliction itself is the kind that, if carried on long enough, would end a life. Going without food and drink does that. Other discomforts, like sitting in the sun, do not.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you wish to say': a phrase that opens an extra proof, in case the earlier one is not convincing
'And I will destroy': from the verse about the punishment for one who breaks יום כיפור
Destruction of the soul, meaning loss of life
Affliction, the special מצוה of יום כיפור

phrases.english: And if you wish to say [something against this],
surely it says:
"I will destroy that soul" (Vayikra 23:30),
phrases.notes: The verse describing the punishment for doing מלאכה on יום כיפור.

phrases.english: [meaning] an affliction that is a destruction of the soul,
and which one is that?
That is [refraining from] eating and drinking.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא's main question, which מצוה of affliction the Torah means, and adds a second proof.
steps.raayaObject: That the עינוי of יום כיפור means not eating and drinking.

steps.title: Why was the extra proof needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what weakness in the earlier proof made the ברייתא say 'and if you wish to say'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'and if you wish to say' mean here?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask what problem the ברייתא saw that made it need a second proof. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'and if you wish to say' suggests that someone could have objected to the first proof. The גמרא wants to know exactly what that objection would be.

phrases.english: What is [meant by] "and if you wish to say"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why the ברייתא's extra proof in step 15 was needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What gap in the first proof the phrase 'and if you wish to say' is meant to close.

steps.title: Someone might think the verse means avoiding forbidden relations
steps.stepSummary: Someone might have said the affliction means avoiding forbidden relations. 'I will destroy that soul' shows it must be an affliction that can kill, which is not eating and drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you would say the verse is talking about forbidden relations, the verse says 'I will destroy that soul.' That means an affliction that can cost a life. Which one is that? Not eating and drinking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the objection the extra proof answers. Someone might think the עינוי means holding back from forbidden relations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding back from relations can also be called 'affliction.' So one might have said that is what the verse means. But holding back from relations never kills anyone, while going without food and drink can. So 'destroying the soul' points only to eating and drinking.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you would say': brings up a possible mistaken idea

phrases.english: And if you would say:
the verse is speaking about forbidden relations,
surely it says:
"I will destroy the soul,"
[meaning] an affliction that involves loss of life,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵי זֶה זֶה? זֶה אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה.
phrases.english: and which one is that? That is [refraining from] eating and drinking.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: בַּעֲרָיוֹת קָא מִישְׁתַּעֵי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra proof rules out the idea that the עינוי means avoiding forbidden relations, since only going without food and drink can cost a life.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל's school: learn from the hunger in the desert
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל learns through a גזירה שוה. The word עינוי appears both here and in the story of the desert, where it means hunger, so here too it means hunger.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: the word 'affliction' is said here, and 'affliction' is said elsewhere. Just as there it means hunger, here too it means hunger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different way to prove that the עינוי of יום כיפור means not eating. It compares the same word used in another verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In דברים 8:3 the תורה says 'He afflicted you and made you hungry,' about the Jews in the desert. Since the same word עינוי is used for יום כיפור, we borrow its meaning: hunger. This is a proof from matching words, not from the punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The school of רבי ישמעאל taught': introduces a teaching from his study hall
'It says here... and it says there': the wording of a גזירה שוה, a comparison of the same word in two verses

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a second, independent source for the main rule of יום כיפור: the basic affliction is going without food.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"affliction" is said here [about Yom Kippur],
and "affliction" is said there [about the desert].
phrases.notes: דברים 8:3: 'He afflicted you and made you hungry.'

phrases.english: Just as there, the affliction is hunger,
so too here, the affliction is hunger.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל תָּנָא: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן עִנּוּי, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן עִנּוּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source for the same rule proven in steps 15 to 17.
steps.raayaObject: That the עינוי of יום כיפור means not eating.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A גזירה שוה from דברים 8:3, the hunger in the desert.

steps.title: Why not learn from לבן's warning to יעקב?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the comparison. Why not compare instead to 'if you afflict my daughters,' where עינוי refers to marital relations?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us learn from 'If you afflict my daughters' instead!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the גזירה שוה. There is another verse with the word עינוי that would point to a different meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In בראשית 31:50, לבן warns יעקב not to afflict his daughters, which refers to holding back marital relations. If we compared to that verse, the עינוי of יום כיפור would mean avoiding relations, not avoiding food. So why choose the desert verse?

keyTerms.meaning: 'And let us learn': suggests a different source to learn from
'If you afflict my daughters': לבן's warning to יעקב (Bereishis 31:50)

phrases.english: But let us learn from "If you afflict my daughters"?
phrases.notes: In that verse, the affliction refers to marital relations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the choice of verse in the גזירה שוה of step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: Comparing יום כיפור to the desert verse rather than to another verse using the same word.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word עינוי also appears in 'If you afflict my daughters,' where it means holding back relations. That would give the opposite result.

steps.title: Learn a group's affliction from a group's affliction
steps.stepSummary: The affliction of יום כיפור is commanded to the whole people. So it is learned from the desert, which also involved the whole people, and not from a case about individuals.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn the affliction of a group from the affliction of a group. We do not learn the affliction of a group from the affliction of an individual.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and explains why the desert verse is the better match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יום כיפור's affliction applies to all of Israel together, just like the hunger in the desert. לבן's warning was about specific individuals, יעקב's wives. A comparison works best between cases that are alike, so the desert verse wins.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We learn': we draw a comparison from one case to another

steps.whatToRemember: The עינוי of יום כיפור at its core means not eating and drinking. We know this from 'I will destroy that soul' (only hunger and thirst can kill) and from the hunger in the desert. The 'group from a group' reason given here is challenged in the next step and replaced in step 22.

phrases.english: We learn the affliction of a group
from the affliction of a group,
and we do not learn the affliction of a group
from the affliction of an individual.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Picks the closer comparison: the two cases must be alike, group with group.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any verse with the word עינוי could be used, including the one about יעקב's wives.
steps.terutzMaskana: A group's affliction is learned only from a group's affliction, so we learn from the hunger in the desert.

steps.title: Why not learn from the affliction in Egypt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the previous answer. The affliction in Egypt also happened to the whole people, yet it meant separation from marital relations.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us learn instead from the affliction of Egypt, as it says 'And He saw our affliction,' and we explain that this means separation from marital relations!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer. That answer said we learn from the desert because the desert involved the whole people. But Egypt also involved the whole people, and there עינוי meant no marital relations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said a public command must be learned from a public case of עינוי. Egypt is also a public case, but there the עינוי was avoiding relations, not hunger. So the 'public' reason alone cannot explain why we pick hunger.

phrases.english: And let us learn from the affliction of Egypt,
as it is written: 'And He saw our affliction,'
and we say: this is separation from marital relations!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 20 with a counter-example that also involves the whole people
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a public עינוי must be learned from the public case of the desert
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Egypt was also public, yet its עינוי meant no marital relations, so the public argument does not lead to hunger

steps.title: Affliction from Heaven is learned from affliction from Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new answer. We compare an affliction from Heaven only to another affliction from Heaven, never to one caused by people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: we learn an affliction from Heaven from another affliction from Heaven, and we do not learn an affliction from Heaven from an affliction caused by people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a new rule for choosing which verse to compare.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hunger in the desert was brought by ה׳, and the fast of יום כיפור is commanded by ה׳. The affliction in Egypt was done by the Egyptians, who are people. So the matching comparison is the desert, which means hunger.

keyTerms.meaning: By the hand of Heaven, from ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: The fast of יום כיפור (no eating or drinking) is learned from the hunger in the desert because both come from Heaven. Egypt's affliction came from people, so it does not count.
steps.confusionAlert: The word 'אלא' signals a change of approach. The גמרא drops the 'public versus private' reason from step 20, which Egypt disproved, and replaces it with a new reason: Heaven versus people.

phrases.english: Rather: we derive affliction by the hand of Heaven
from affliction by the hand of Heaven,
and we do not derive affliction by the hand of Heaven
from affliction by the hand of man.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא: דָּנִין עִנּוּי בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם מֵעִנּוּי בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Egypt
steps.terutzResolutionType: New criterion for choosing the comparison (source of the affliction)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Egypt is a public affliction, so it could be the model, and then עינוי would mean no marital relations
steps.terutzMaskana: Only an affliction from Heaven like the desert hunger can be the model, so עינוי means not eating or drinking
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The עינוי of יום כיפור means hunger, learned from the Heaven-sent hunger in the desert

steps.title: How was eating the manna an affliction?
steps.stepSummary: Since the desert verse came up, the גמרא asks why the Torah calls eating the מן an 'affliction.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Who feeds you manna in the desert... in order to afflict you.' How was this an affliction?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a side topic connected to the desert verse. It quotes a verse that calls the מן an affliction and asks what that means. This sets up the answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מן was miraculous food from Heaven, so calling it an 'affliction' is surprising. The question is about understanding the verse. It is not an attack on any earlier step.

keyTerms.meaning: The manna, the food from Heaven in the desert

phrases.english: 'Who feeds you manna in the desert
... in order to afflict you'? (What affliction was this?)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Side discussion prompted by the desert verse used in the גזירה שוה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the affliction in eating the מן was

steps.title: Two explanations of the manna's affliction
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי disagree. One says the problem was having no food stored for tomorrow. The other says it was eating food you cannot see as it tastes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי and רבי אסי: One said, someone who has bread in his basket is not like someone who has no bread in his basket. The other said, someone who sees what he eats is not like someone who does not see what he eats.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give two different answers to the question of how the מן was an affliction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First view: the מן came one day at a time, so people worried about tomorrow. Second view: the מן tasted like any food you wanted but always looked the same, so you never saw the food you were tasting. Both describe a kind of mild 'hunger' even while eating.

keyTerms.meaning: One said (we are not told which sage)
It is not the same as
Bread in his basket, food saved for later

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi disagreed:
One said: there is no comparison between
one who has bread in his basket
and one who has no bread in his basket,
and one said: there is no comparison between
one who sees and eats
and one who does not see and eats.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַמֵּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי, חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either no food stored for tomorrow, or not seeing the food that matches its taste

steps.title: A hint about blind people
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף learns from the second view that blind people eat but do not feel fully satisfied.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: from here there is a hint that blind people eat but are not satisfied.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף draws a lesson from the view that seeing your food matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If not seeing the food made the מן an affliction, then seeing is part of feeling full. So a blind person, who cannot see his food, does not feel fully satisfied.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
from here there is a hint regarding the blind,
that they eat and are not satisfied.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: מִכָּאן רֶמֶז לְסוֹמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the second opinion of step 24
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seeing food is part of being satisfied, so the blind eat without full satisfaction

steps.title: Eat your meal in daylight
steps.stepSummary: אביי gives practical advice: eat a meal only by day, when you can see it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: therefore, whoever has a meal should eat it only in the daytime.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי turns רב יוסף's idea into practical advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since seeing the food adds to satisfaction, one should eat a meal when there is light. Then he gets the full benefit of the food.

phrases.english: Abaye said: therefore,
one who has a meal
should eat it only in the daytime.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Practical consequence of step 25
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eat a meal by daylight so you can see your food

steps.title: A verse for the value of seeing
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא brings a verse from קהלת as the source for the idea that seeing satisfies.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: what is the verse? 'Better is the seeing of the eyes than the wandering of the desire.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא supports the idea of the last steps with a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says that seeing with the eyes is better than desire that wanders. This supports the claim that seeing your food adds to satisfaction.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said: what is the verse?
'Better is the seeing of the eyes than the wandering of the desire.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a verse to support steps 25-26
steps.raayaObject: The idea that seeing food adds to satisfaction

steps.title: Another use of the same verse
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש uses the same verse for a different teaching: looking at a woman gives more pleasure than the act itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: the sight of a woman is better than the act itself, as it says: 'Better is the seeing of the eyes than the wandering of the desire.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש explains the same verse in a different area. Seeing is more powerful than the act itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This teaching is linked here because it uses the same verse. It shows how strongly the eyes affect desire and pleasure. It also connects back to the earlier idea that seeing matters.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (in a verse)

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
the sight of the eyes upon a woman is better
than the act itself,
as it is stated: 'Better is the seeing of the eyes than the wandering of the desire.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: טוֹב מַרְאֵה עֵינַיִם בְּאִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching on the same verse
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sight has a stronger effect than the act itself

steps.title: A new dispute about a verse on wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another disagreement between רבי אמי and רבי אסי, about a verse on wine. This passage ends in the middle of the first opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'When he puts his eye in the cup, it goes smoothly.' רבי אמי and רבי אסי: one said, whoever puts...
steps.whatsHappening: Because רבי אמי and רבי אסי argued about one verse, the גמרא brings another verse they argued about. This is a setup line, and the explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This starts a new side topic, linked only because the same two sages disagree. The verse speaks of looking at wine in the cup. The first opinion begins with 'whoever puts' and is finished on the next amud.

phrases.english: 'When it gives its eye (color) in the cup,
it goes down smoothly,'
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi disagreed:
one said: whoever puts (his eyes)...

steps.triggerLanguage: ״כִּי יִתֵּן בַּכּוֹס עֵינוֹ יִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּמֵישָׁרִים״, רַבִּי אַמֵּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Linked to step 24 because the same two sages disagree
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opening of a dispute on Proverbs 23:31, which continues on the next amud
